stances.claim: The US Electoral College -- 538 electors with 270 needed to win, allocated to states by population and governed (in 48 of 50 states + DC) by winner-takes-all -- is a 'complex, indirect system' under which a candidate 'may capture a majority of the popular vote yet lose the electoral vote.' This has happened five times: 1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016.

The 2000 Bush v. Gore SCOTUS decision (5-4) refusing the Florida manual recount of 'imperfectly punched automated ballots' was 'lampooned for being partisan' -- given that Florida's governor was George's brother Jeb, the state electoral commission was headed by a Bush-appointed Cabinet member, and the five anti-Gore justices were all Republican-appointed while the four pro-Gore were all Democratic-appointed.

Despite the 'widespread howling,' Gore 'humbly accepted the decision and conceded defeat' -- and in a 2006 private conversation with CJ Panganiban explained his reasoning: 'There is something greater than me. The survival of our democratic institutions is more important than my personal victory. The Supreme Court had spoken. Though I disagreed with its decision, I had a duty to respect and obey it.' Rule of law at its best.

The Electoral College's structural logic is 'theoretical parity among the states of the Union' -- reflected also in the 100-member Senate (2 per state regardless of population) -- which makes the Union 'democratic' in the same way that 'the sovereign equality of independent states in the United Nations gives every member one vote,' so populous India (>1 billion) is the 'sovereign equal' of small Singapore (<6 million).

notable_anecdotes: The Gore 2006 Manila private conversation: CJ asks 'Why did you not pursue your remedies in the public fora and in the streets of America?' and Gore answers -- 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me. The survival of our democratic institutions is more important than my personal victory... If I had protracted the battle to America's streets and parks, there would have been chaos and political upheaval. The manual recount would have taken many months. Meanwhile, no one would have been sworn in as President that ensuing January. Can you imagine a leaderless United States?' -- followed by CJ's one-line acclamation 'Rule of law at its best!' The encounter is the column's emotional and doctrinal centerpiece.

The 2000 Bush v. Gore partisan-pattern documentation: governor of Florida = Jeb Bush (George's brother); state electoral commission head = Cabinet appointee of the governor; five anti-Gore justices all Republican-appointed; four pro-Gore all Democratic-appointed -- preserved with deliberate completeness to highlight the partisan signature of the 5-4 outcome.
The 2016 Clinton 'three million more popular votes' losing electorally 304-227 -- preserved as the most recent mismatch evidence prompting the 2020 'undemocratic?' critique that E59 later answers.
Sovereign-equality UN analogy: India (>1 billion) and Singapore (<6 million) as equal members -- concretizing the abstract argument for state-equality balancing.

one_paragraph_summary: Two days before the November 3, 2020 US election, Panganiban explains 'the race to 270' between Joe Biden (78) and Donald Trump (74). US voters do not elect the president directly -- they elect 'electors' (538 in total, allocated to the 50 states and DC in rough proportion to population: California has 55; Alaska, Montana, Wyoming, and DC have three each), and a candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win. Most states (all except Maine and Nebraska) apply a winner-takes-all rule, awarding their full electoral slate to the popular-vote plurality winner. Each state legislature determines its own elector-selection process, but Election Day is fixed (first Tuesday after the first Monday of November) and the winner is sworn in on January 20. Under this complex, indirect system, a candidate may win the nationwide popular vote yet lose the electoral vote -- which has happened in five elections (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016). In 2016, Hillary Clinton won three million more popular votes than Trump but lost the electoral vote 304-227. The most controversial mismatch was 2000: Al Gore won the popular vote but lost 271-266 to George W. Bush after the US Supreme Court, voting 5-4, rejected a manual recount of 'imperfectly punched automated ballots' in Florida. CJ notes the partisan pattern: Florida's governor was Jeb Bush (George's brother), the state electoral commission was headed by a Bush-appointed Cabinet member, and the five anti-Gore justices were all Republican-appointed while the four pro-Gore were all Democratic-appointed. Yet Gore 'humbly accepted the decision and conceded defeat.' During CJ's CJ-tenure in 2006, Gore visited Manila and in a private conversation answered CJ's question why he had not taken his remedies to America's streets: 'Mr. Chief Justice, there is something greater than me. The survival of our democratic institutions is more important than my personal victory. The Supreme Court had spoken. Though I disagreed with its decision, I had a duty to respect and obey it... Can you imagine a leaderless United States?' -- to which CJ appends, 'Rule of law at its best!' Structurally, the Electoral College's 'theoretical parity among the states' -- reflected also in the 100-member Senate (two per state regardless of population) -- makes the Union 'democratic' in the same way that 'the sovereign equality of independent states in the United Nations gives every member one vote,' so India (>1 billion people) is the sovereign equal of Singapore (<6 million).
